# Comparative language histories: 12 profiles

Profiles: [Spanish](spanish.md), [Fijian](fijian.md), [Mandarin](mandarin.md), [Yoruba](yoruba.md), [Hebrew](hebrew.md), [Georgian](georgian.md), [Khmer](khmer.md), [Hindi](hindi.md), [Aramaic](aramaic.md), [Proto-Oceanic](proto-oceanic.md), [Ancient Egyptian](egyptian.md), [Mycenaean Greek recorded in Linear B](linear-b-mycenaean.md). Research navigation: [five original profiles](research/README.md) and [seven additions](research/extended/README.md). The original stable code API remains at `Onyx/js/language-history/research/index.js`; additions are in `extended-index.js`.

| Choice | Historical root or early stage | Sibling comparison | Dating caution |
|---|---|---|---|
| Spanish | Archaic Latin inscriptions, seventh–sixth c. BCE | Romance descendants including Portuguese/Galician and broader Romance relatives | Spanish formed later; inscriptions date Latin writing, not modern Spanish |
| Fijian | Proto-Oceanic c. 3,000–3,300 BP (1950 baseline) calibration | Fijian varieties and Polynesian through later Central Pacific history | Archaeology-informed model, not direct language attestation |
| Mandarin | Sino-Tibetan root estimates c. 5,871–7,983 BP; Old Chinese written evidence in Late Shang | Sinitic branches including Wu, Yue, Min, Hakka, Gan, Xiang, Jin and others; wider Tibeto-Burman comparisons | Modeled family dates vary; neither Shang writing nor the family root dates Mandarin directly |
| Yoruba | Niger-Congo expansion estimate near 12,000 BP; local Proto-Yoruboid model 2500–300 BCE | Itsekiri, Igala and Yoruba varieties | Macrofamily expansion is broad and classification-sensitive; local range is model-specific |
| Hebrew | Canaanite evidence c. 1550–1200 BCE; Hebrew differentiates gradually near Late Bronze / Early Iron | Phoenician, Ammonite, Moabite, Edomite; Aramaic close but distinct | Gradual boundary, not a single founding date |
| Georgian | Proto-Kartvelian; comparative estimates include 3,950–4,750 BP, while a separate model proposes >12,500 BP | Svan, Mingrelian, Laz | The 3,950 BP audit value is the low end of cited comparative estimates, not consensus |
| Khmer | Proto-Austroasiatic modeled at 3,000–4,500 BP | Mon, Vietnamese, Khasi and other Austroasiatic branches | Macrofamily chronology and subgrouping remain debated |
| Hindi | Proto-Indo-Aryan; Vedic oral texts from c. 1500 BCE | Urdu/Hindustani, Punjabi, Gujarati, Bengali, Marathi | Not a direct Sanskrit-to-Hindi line |
| Aramaic | Northwest Semitic; Old Aramaic inscriptions by 10th–9th c. BCE | Hebrew, Phoenician, Ugaritic; later Aramaic branches | Earliest inscription dates are debated |
| Proto-Oceanic | Reconstructed at c. 3,000–3,300 BP | Central Pacific, Micronesian, Admiralty and western Oceanic branches | Comparative reconstruction, no native written record |
| Ancient Egyptian | Proto-Afroasiatic estimates vary roughly 8,000–15,000+ BP | Semitic, Berber, Cushitic, Chadic, Omotic | Root date estimates are deeply contested; Egyptian records attest a later daughter branch |
| Mycenaean Greek / Linear B | Proto-Greek ancestor; Mycenaean written c. 1450–1150 BCE | Arcado-Cypriot, Attic-Ionic, Aeolic, Doric | Linear B is the script, Mycenaean Greek the language |

Age refers to an ancestor or an attested historical stage, not an unchanged modern language. Reconstructed stages are hypotheses. Inscriptions, archaeology-calibrated phylogenies and manuscript dates are different kinds of evidence. Unicode encodes characters and marks, not pen strokes or stroke order.

## Extended atlas

Seven additional source-linked dossiers are available in [the extended research atlas](research/extended/README.md), with a separate executable index and validator. The atlas includes an [evidence and dating methodology](research/extended/evidence-methodology.md) separating reconstructed ancestor dates from written or oral attestation and script chronology.

entries.content:
# Fijian: Oceanic ancestry, open syllables and orthography
Proto-Oceanic is calibrated around 3,000–3,300 BP; Proto-Central Pacific is later and differentiated around Fiji. Proto-Polynesian branched eastward. Fijian itself has eastern/western varieties; Rotuman’s exact placement is debated. These dates are models, not written attestations.

19th-century missionaries developed the Latin-based standard, with Bauan influence; print and Bible translation helped stabilize it. Letter mappings include b /mb/, d /nd/, q /ŋɡ/, g /ŋ/, c /ð/. Dr represents a rhotic sound with differing phonetic analyses. Standard writing generally needs no diacritics; academic macrons may mark length. There are no native subscripts. Unicode stores letters, not strokes.

Fijian favors open CV/V syllables and commonly penultimate stress. Basic transitive clauses are often VOS/verb-initial. Comparative examples: Proto-Oceanic *p > /v/ in Bauan *patu ‘stone’ > vatu; *s > /t/ in cited Lau examples such as *pose ‘paddle’. The latter is Lau-specific.

Sources: [ANU Press](https://press-files.anu.edu.au/downloads/press/p69411/html/ch03.html); [dating study](https://academic.oup.com/jole/article/5/1/17/5688948); [Schütz, The Fijian Language](https://manifold.uhpress.hawaii.edu/projects/the-fijian-language); [Cambridge Fiji missionaries](https://maa.cam.ac.uk/Fiji-missionaries).\n

# Hebrew: Canaanite inheritance and script succession
Canaanite is attested c.1550–1200 BCE; Hebrew differentiated around the Late Bronze/Iron transition, roughly 3,200 years ago. Phoenician, Ammonite, Moabite and Edomite are close siblings. Ugaritic is related Northwest Semitic but normally outside narrower Canaanite. The boundary is gradual.

Early Hebrew used Phoenician-derived Paleo-Hebrew. An Aramaic-derived square script became dominant in the Persian period; Paleo-Hebrew persisted in some contexts. Masoretic readers added niqqud vowel points and cantillation marks; modern everyday text usually omits them. Hebrew is RTL with 22 consonants. Block U+0590–U+05FF; final forms ך U+05DA, ם U+05DD, ן U+05DF, ף U+05E3, ץ U+05E5. Niqqud are combining marks (e.g. sheva U+05B0, qamats U+05B8), not subscripts. Unicode does not encode physical strokes.

Modern syllables often (C)(C)V(C). Many Israeli speakers merge historical emphatics/pharyngeals; /ħ/ may merge with /x/, /ʔ/ may be lost, and gemination is commonly absent. Biblical clauses often verb-initial; Modern Hebrew commonly SVO with fronting. Root-pattern binyanim and construct state are central.

Sources: [Cambridge Hebrew](https://www.cambridge.org/core/books/abs/ancient-languages-of-syriapalestine-and-arabia/hebrew/512F0FC4796BF3DB1137C1A9BA228DB1); [UT Austin Canaanite](https://sites.utexas.edu/scripts/files/2020/10/2019-AWW-The-Canaanite-Languages.pdf); [Modern Hebrew phonology](https://cris.biu.ac.il/en/publications/notes-on-modern-hebrew-phonology-and-orthography/); [Unicode Hebrew](https://www.unicode.org/charts/PDF/U0590.pdf).\n

entries.content:
# Mandarin: Old Chinese, Sinitic siblings and Han writing
Late Shang oracle-bone records attest Old Chinese c.1250–1045 BCE. This dates texts/artifacts, not speech origins. Sinitic sibling groupings commonly include Jin, Wu, Gan, Xiang, Hakka, Yue, Min, Hui and Pinghua; classification counts vary. Middle Chinese evidence preserves richer codas and tone categories; 1324 Zhongyuan Yinyun documents Old Mandarin. PRC adopted Pinyin in 1958.

Chinese script history includes oracle bone, bronze, seal, clerical, regular, running and cursive forms. Han characters are morphosyllabic; Pinyin is an auxiliary Romanization. Simplified and traditional forms coexist. Unicode Han main block U+4E00–U+9FFF. Pinyin ā U+0101, á U+00E1, ǎ U+01CE, à U+00E0; combining tone marks U+0304/0301/030C/0300; ü U+00FC. Stroke order is not encoded; no native subscripts.

Modern syllable template roughly (C)(G)V(X), with nasal codas and four lexical tones plus neutral tone. Mandarin lost Middle Chinese final /p t k/, redistributing entering-tone items. Earlier onset voicing conditioned tone splits across Sinitic. Modern Mandarin is broadly SVO/topic-comment; particles, aspect, classifiers and coverbs are key.

Sources: [Oxford writing origins](https://academic.oup.com/book/58672/chapter/485387630); [Smithsonian oracle bone](https://asia.si.edu/education/educator-resources/teaching-china-with-the-smithsonian/explore-by-object/inscribed-tortoise-shell-oracle-bone/); [Cambridge historical phonology](https://www.cambridge.org/core/books/abs/phonological-history-of-chinese/an-introduction-to-chinese-historical-phonology/7A1DECBDCB0C27F0486F3409A697D592); [MOE Pinyin](https://www.moe.gov.cn/jyb_sjzl/ziliao/A19/195802/t19580201_186000.html); [Unicode CJK](https://www.unicode.org/charts/PDF/U4E00.pdf).\n

# Five language histories: expanded research set

This is the second, deeper pass on the five existing Onyx language tracks. It keeps the established selections: Spanish (Romance), Fijian (Oceanic), Mandarin Chinese (Asian / Sinitic), Yoruba (African) and Hebrew (Middle Eastern). Each language has five focused research notes and six JavaScript modules. Shared modules provide source-linked aggregation, Unicode inspection, comparison and validation.

## Browse the research

| Language | Research notes | Main comparison branches | Root-age evidence |
|---|---|---|---|
| Spanish | [Spanish notes](spanish/) | Portuguese/Galician, Astur-Leonese, Aragonese and wider Romance | Early Latin inscriptions; Spanish itself is medieval |
| Fijian | [Fijian notes](fijian/) | Fijian varieties and Polynesian through Central Pacific; Rotuman placement is cautious | Archaeology-calibrated Proto-Oceanic, about 3,000–3,300 BP |
| Mandarin | [Mandarin notes](mandarin/) | Sinitic branches and wider Sino-Tibetan comparison; subgroup labels vary | Bayesian Sino-Tibetan root estimates; Shang writing is separate and does not date Mandarin |
| Yoruba | [Yoruba notes](yoruba/) | Igala, Itsekiri and Yoruba varieties | Niger-Congo expansion estimate about 12,000 BP with contested deep classification; local Proto-Yoruboid model remains broad |
| Hebrew | [Hebrew notes](hebrew/) | Phoenician, Ammonite, Moabite and Edomite; Aramaic is a close relative | Canaanite evidence and gradual Hebrew differentiation in the Late Bronze / Early Iron transition |

## What the code contains

The JavaScript folders under `Onyx/js/language-history/research/` store family trees, chronology rows with evidence classes, scoped sound correspondences, syllable/sentence summaries and script/Unicode examples. Each record carries direct sources and caution text. The existing flat language modules remain the Onyx entry points and are extended with the research bundle. The common [index](../../../js/language-history/research/index.js) exports the five profiles; [validation](../../../js/language-history/research/validate.js) checks source coverage and Unicode examples.

## Reading dates correctly

An attested inscription dates a written object; a proto-language is reconstructed from correspondences; archaeology may calibrate a migration model; a modern spelling standard has its own institutional history. The five dates are not interchangeable. Every root-age note identifies what the date applies to and how confident the attribution is. Mandarin’s root age is a modeled Sino-Tibetan family estimate, separate from Shang writing and Mandarin; Yoruba’s deep macrofamily expansion estimate is broad and classification-sensitive, while the local Proto-Yoruboid window is explicitly model-specific.

See the [root-age criteria and model audit](root-age-criteria.md) for the 2,500-year floor, evidence types and machine-readable checks.

## Unicode and glyphs

The language files identify native letters, diacritics, tone marks, vowel points, final forms, auxiliary romanizations and code points. Unicode code points do not encode handwriting strokes or stroke order. A combining sequence can form one user-perceived grapheme; normalize text consistently, preserve language-distinctive marks, and do not treat below-base diacritics as subscript letters. See [Unicode and glyph method](unicode-and-glyph-method.md).

# Five-system comparison: what should be compared

| Language | Broad syllable profile | Sentence tendencies | Main script | Marks and encoding detail |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Spanish | (C)(C)V(C), with segmental and dialect restrictions | Neutral SVO, flexible order, frequent null subjects | Latin | ñ, acute accents, ü, inverted punctuation |
| Fijian | Open V/CV; penultimate-mora stress | Verb-initial / often VOS in transitive clauses | Latin-based standard | Unusual letter-to-sound values; few required diacritics |
| Mandarin | (C)(G)V(X), restricted nasal finals; lexical tones | SVO and topic-comment | Han characters; Pinyin auxiliary | Pinyin tone marks and ü; Unicode CJK ideographs |
| Yoruba | Traditional V/CV and syllabic nasals; modern loan strata vary | SVO, preverbal markers, serial verbs | Adapted Latin; Ajami also used | Under-dots plus tone marks; stacked combining sequences |
| Hebrew | Modern broad (C)(C)V(C), earlier stages differ | Biblical clauses often VSO; modern Hebrew commonly SVO | Paleo-Hebrew then square Hebrew | Niqqud, cantillation, final forms and RTL handling |

The formulas are teaching summaries, not parsers. Mandarin characters are not alphabetic letters; Fijian b is not /b/ in the English value; Yoruba dot-below changes letter identity; Hebrew vowel points are later reading marks; Spanish ñ is an alphabet letter. Identical Unicode concepts can serve different linguistic functions. Compare languages at matched levels (ancestor with ancestor, modern norm with modern norm) and name dialect/period for each claim.

## Sources

- [Cambridge Handbook of Spanish Linguistics, The Syllable](https://www.cambridge.org/core/books/abs/cambridge-handbook-of-spanish-linguistics/syllable/CB48DEE6ECF4EAD91E816486BA8E8573)
- [The Fijian Language](https://manifold.uhpress.hawaii.edu/projects/the-fijian-language)
- [Oxford Handbook of Chinese Linguistics, Sinitic classification](https://academic.oup.com/edited-volume/38607/chapter-abstract/334718815)
- [Emerging Grammars in Contemporary Yoruba Phonology](https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/canadian-journal-of-linguistics-revue-canadienne-de-linguistique/article/emerging-grammars-in-contemporary-yoruba-phonology/5FBC31A5B98304BD5F4F398569D75854)

entries.content:
# Evidence and dating method

## Separate the clocks

This set uses four evidence classes: (1) inscriptions and dated manuscripts, (2) reconstructed linguistic stages based on regular correspondences, (3) archaeological or Bayesian family-date calibrations, and (4) social/orthographic milestones such as printing, school standards or official Romanization. Each module labels the kind of date it reports. A dated written object proves that a form was written by then; it does not date the origin of speech. A reconstructed proto-language has no surviving direct recording.

## Root-age requirement

The chosen families have ancestor stages older than 2,500 years, but support differs. In dates marked BP, the archaeological baseline is 1950 CE rather than the date this document is read. Latin has archaic inscriptions by the seventh–sixth centuries BCE. Proto-Oceanic uses a documented archaeological calibration of c.3,000–3,300 BP. For Mandarin, Bayesian Sino-Tibetan phylogenies estimate the wider family root at 5,871 BP, 7,184 BP and 7,983 BP in separate studies; this is a model-based date, with a 2020 study reporting a wide 95% highest posterior density interval. Late Shang writing is a separate attestation, not the emergence date of Mandarin. Hebrew’s Canaanite evidence and differentiation are placed around the Late Bronze / Early Iron transition. For Yoruba, one Cambridge overview places Niger-Congo expansion near 12,000 BP, while its internal classification and reconstruction remain debated; a closer Proto-Yoruboid model gives a broad 2500–300 BCE period and daughter differentiation around 300 CE. Neither is a precise inscription date, and the local window is not consensus glottochronology. These differences are exposed rather than compressed into false precision.

## Family trees and siblings

Siblings are branches sharing a reconstructed ancestor, not necessarily mutually intelligible languages. For Mandarin, subgroup labels and whether Jin is grouped with Mandarin vary, and the root models concern Sino-Tibetan rather than a Mandarin-specific split. Fijian is internally diverse and Polynesian is a nearby Central Pacific branch. Yoruboid higher and lower classifications are still discussed, and Niger-Congo is a macrofamily with contested deep structure. Ugaritic is Northwest Semitic, but its inclusion in narrow Canaanite classifications varies. These caveats are part of the evidence, not omissions.

## Sound correspondences

Every sound-change record names its source stage, environment, outcome, example and limitation. A comparison such as Latin *f* weakening in Castilian, Proto-Oceanic *p* : Bauan Fijian *v*, a Mandarin coda-tone change, the Canaanite vowel shift, or a Yoruba loanword syllable repair has a specific period and scope. The records are not transformations to run on arbitrary words.

## Sources

- [Best practices in justifying calibrations for dating language families](https://doi.org/10.1093/jole/lzz009)
- [Cambridge, The Indo-European Language Family: Italic](https://www.cambridge.org/core/books/indoeuropean-language-family/italic/473A395FABB6E9FB91AE75076F390D29)
- [Cambridge, Hebrew](https://www.cambridge.org/core/books/abs/ancient-languages-of-syriapalestine-and-arabia/hebrew/512F0FC4796BF3DB1137C1A9BA228DB1)
- [Cambridge, The Yoruba from Prehistory to the Present](https://www.cambridge.org/core/books/yoruba-from-prehistory-to-the-present/geography-and-society/CC682B3D24A7A9648C018BABC1E2EDEA)
- [The Yoruba: A New History](https://iupress.org/9780253051486/the-yoruba/)
- [Y13: Good, Niger-Congo languages](https://doi.org/10.1017/9781107279872.018)
- [Y14: East Benue-Congo, Language Science Press](https://langsci-press.org/catalog/view/190/1074/1266-2)

# Extended language atlas

Seven profiles extend the original comparative atlas: Georgian, Khmer, Hindi, Aramaic, reconstructed Proto-Oceanic, Ancient Egyptian, and Mycenaean Greek recorded in Linear B. The last item is deliberately labeled as a language/script distinction: Linear B is not a language. Proto-Oceanic is reconstructed and has no native script.

Each profile has five linked, source-backed topic notes and six JavaScript modules (five data modules plus an index). Read [Evidence, dates, and comparison labels](evidence-methodology.md) for the distinctions between reconstructed roots, surviving records, language relationships, scripts, Unicode code points, and glyph rendering. Root-age evidence records its method, documentary status, range interpretation, source keys, and confidence; validation is separate from the original five-profile API.

| Profile | Family | Root/stage used for age test | Main caution |
|---|---|---|---|
| [Georgian (Kartuli)](georgian/README.md) | Kartvelian | Proto-Kartvelian (3,950 BP low comparative estimate; separate >12,500 BP model) | very low for exact dating; estimates are not a confidence interval |
| [Khmer (Modern Khmer; historical Old Khmer)](khmer/README.md) | Austroasiatic | Proto-Austroasiatic (3000–4500 BP) | contested model; low confidence in exact chronology and homeland |
| [Hindi (Modern Standard Hindi; Hindustani continuum)](hindi/README.md) | Indo-European | Proto-Indo-Aryan (with deeper Proto-Indo-Iranian comparison) (3200–3800 BP) | moderate for Vedic attestation horizon; lower for exact proto-stage dating |
| [Aramaic (historical language continuum)](aramaic/README.md) | Afroasiatic | Proto-Northwest Semitic → Aramaic branch (Old Aramaic attested) (2500–3500 BP) | high for early first-millennium BCE written evidence; branch boundaries and exact first dates are debated |
| [Proto-Oceanic (POc; reconstructed ancestor, not a living language)](proto-oceanic/README.md) | Austronesian | Proto-Oceanic (3000–3300 BP) | moderate as an archaeology-informed reconstruction; subgroup boundaries and dates vary |
| [Ancient Egyptian (historical stages; Afroasiatic)](egyptian/README.md) | Afroasiatic | Proto-Afroasiatic (deep reconstructed ancestor; proposals 8,000–15,000+ BP) | very low for exact deep dates and homeland; proposed dates differ by millennia |
| [Mycenaean Greek (recorded in Linear B; script/language distinguished)](linear-b-mycenaean/README.md) | Indo-European | Proto-Greek / early Greek dialect continuum (3400–4000 BP) | moderate for chronology of Greek presence and linguistic identification; exact Proto-Greek split date is modeled |

Run `node Onyx/js/language-history/research/validate-extended.js` to check extended module sources, Unicode examples, and root-age evidence.

entries.content:
## Family placement

Aramaic is Northwest Semitic within Semitic and Afroasiatic. It is historically diverse: Old, Imperial/Official, Middle, and later Eastern and Western varieties are labels for phases and traditions, not one homogeneous language at all dates. Its close comparisons include Hebrew and Phoenician, but Aramaic is not a form of Hebrew. Many Jewish, Christian, and regional literary traditions used distinct Aramaic dialects.

**Proposed root:** Proto-Northwest Semitic → Aramaic branch (Old Aramaic attested) — 2500–3500 BP, using 1950 CE as the conventional BP origin. The qualifying point estimate is 2850 BP. Confidence: high for early first-millennium BCE written evidence; branch boundaries and exact first dates are debated. This date concerns the stated ancestor; it is not an age claim for the modern language. 

**Siblings and comparisons:**
- Hebrew (Northwest Semitic; Canaanite)
- Phoenician (Northwest Semitic; Canaanite)
- Ugaritic (Northwest Semitic; extinct, distinct branch placement debated)
- Arabic (Central Semitic, not a dialect of Aramaic)
- Modern Aramaic varieties (Neo-Aramaic branches; internal classifications vary)

Do not flatten distant relatives and immediate sister groups into a single branching level.

## Sources

- [A1] [Cambridge History of Iran, Aramaic in the Achaemenian Empire and earliest inscriptions](https://doi.org/10.1017/CHOL9780521200912.016)
- [A2] [Encyclopaedia Iranica, Aramaic language and its history](https://iranicaonline.org/articles/aramaic-i)
- [A3] [Mnamon, Aramaic writing systems and descendants](https://mnamon.sns.it/index.php?id=7&lang=en&page=Scrittura)

## Chronology and evidence

Aramaic inscriptions appear in the early first millennium BCE, with dating and interpretation of the earliest examples actively discussed. Imperial/Official Aramaic spread widely through Neo-Assyrian, Babylonian, and Achaemenid administrative networks, while local spoken varieties continued to diversify. Later branches include Syriac, Jewish Aramaic traditions, Mandaic, and modern Neo-Aramaic varieties; their written histories differ.

**Dating statement:** Proto-Northwest Semitic is reconstructed from shared correspondences and branches including Aramaic and Canaanite; Old Aramaic inscriptions by the tenth–ninth centuries BCE provide a documentary floor. The 2,850 BP value dates the attested branch benchmark, not the exact proto-language split.

Keep three clocks separate: (1) reconstructed ancestor age, (2) earliest surviving written attestation, and (3) emergence of a standardized modern variety. They answer different questions. A lack of early writing is not evidence that a language did not exist.
